newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway cuts rates again, curbs intervention.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway cuts rates again, curbs intervention.

text.p: Norway's central bank, facing a runaway crown, cut official interest rates for the second time in two days on Friday and said it was now curbing interventions in the market.
Effective immediately, the beleaguered bank reduced the deposit rate and the overnight lending rate charged to commercial and savings banks by 25 basis points to 3.25 and 5.25 percent respectively.
Dealers said markets had discounted the cut.

The bank on Wednesday announced a 50 basis point reduction in both rates effective Thursday in a fruitless effort to curb the steady rise of the oil currency, which continued to appreciate after the latest cut.

"The crown exchange rate has recently been under persistent pressure," the bank said in a statement. "Norges Bank (central bank) has purchased foreign currency equivalent to NOK 20 billion since the start of 1997."

The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability. The crown is in a dirty float, which means the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not officially declared.

Announcing a temporary policy shift, the bank said "...in the light of developments in the foreign exchange market, Norges Bank will not intervene to any substantial extent in the foreign exchange market over a period".
Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo, commenting on the bank's decision to curb interventions, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV):

"It means that the crown might be more volatile than we've seen before, that the markets are going to have a closer look at the crown, possibly test it towards the D-mark. It is a tough call today when the markets are moving very rapidly. We are going to see a new level for the crown.

"I expect it to stay there at least in the short term. We would have to see whether economic fundamentals then justify that level or whether we still have what you call an undervalued crown," Stephansen said.

Analysts say the crown is undervalued as the Norwegian economy is booming with huge surpluses in the national budget and current account. Norway is the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.
Undeterred by the cut in official interest rates, the crown powered to its strongest level in more than six years on Thursday on what dealers described as speculative buying.

It outperformed the inverse ECU index of European currencies for the first time. It appreciated from 100.64 on the index shortly before the cut was announced after Norwegian markets closed on Wednesday to 99.89 when they shut on Thursday.
On Friday, after the latest announcement, the crown continued to surge ahead and stood at 98.85 at 0930gmt.
